spme.title: Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME
spme.html:
Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME

SPME approximates Ewald structure factors using smooth cardinal B-splines. Treat it as a specific interpolation-and-force construction rather than a synonym for every PME implementation.

Problem and representative equations

Let uᵢ be particle coordinates in mesh units and Mₚ a cardinal B-spline of order p, not degree p. The product below is the local tensor assignment in three dimensions. Fourier structure factors require a correction for the spline response.

Qmxmymz=∑iqi∏d∈{x,y,z}Mp(uid−md),deg⁡Mp=p−1.Q_{m_xm_ym_z}=\sum_iq_i\prod_{d\in\{x,y,z\}}M_p(u_{id}-m_d),\qquad \deg M_p=p-1.Qmx​my​mz​​=i∑​qi​d∈{x,y,z}∏​Mp​(uid​−md​),degMp​=p−1.

Algorithm

Spread charge over p neighboring mesh points in each direction, evaluate a corrected reciprocal mesh energy by FFT, and obtain forces using derivatives of the assignment in analytical differentiation. Record the spline order and mesh together with whether differentiation is analytical or in Fourier space.

Conditions and pitfalls

Smooth assignment alone does not guarantee both energy consistency and exact net-force cancellation. Ewald neutrality, boundary and self-term conventions still apply. Comparisons with original PME should control error tolerance and differentiation rules, not merely the number of mesh points.

What to check

Measure force errors against the same converged Ewald reference and check energy finite differences. Report common-translation mesh effects and total force separately. Ensure real-space truncation is not hiding the reciprocal-space convergence trend.

slab-ewald.title: Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald
slab-ewald.html:
Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald

Interfaces often require periodicity in two directions and isolation in the normal direction. Elongating a triply periodic cell is not identical to evaluating the genuinely two-periodic Green function.

Problem and representative equations

For a neutral cell of volume V, normal z and unit Coulomb prefactor, the Yeh–Berkowitz correction adds a dipole contribution to a specified three-periodic Ewald baseline. Its coordinate derivative gives the normal force correction. The formula assumes neutrality and a conducting-boundary 3D reference.

Mz=∑iqizi,ΔE=2πVMz2,ΔFi,z=−4πVqiMz.M_z=\sum_iq_i z_i,\qquad \Delta E=\frac{2\pi}{V}M_z^2,\qquad \Delta F_{i,z}=-\frac{4\pi}{V}q_iM_z.Mz​=i∑​qi​zi​,ΔE=V2π​Mz2​,ΔFi,z​=−V4π​qi​Mz​.

Algorithm

Place slabs in an elongated cell with vacuum, converge the 3D sums, and add the dipole correction. Increase the vacuum height to assess residual image interactions. At finite vacuum height, this is not a claim of exact equivalence to a fully two-periodic summation.

Conditions and pitfalls

Charged slabs, other external dielectric conditions, electrodes and imposed fields require additional formulations. Keep self and k=0 conventions distinct from this correction. Neutral-cell M_z is invariant under an origin shift; net charge destroys that property.

What to check

Use neutral charge pairs or a dipole layer and vary vacuum height independently of reciprocal/mesh cutoffs. Compare with an independent two-periodic reference when available, and finite-difference the energy for normal forces. Agreement with an uncorrected 3D calculation cannot establish zero slab error.

fdtd.title: Yee finite-difference time-domain method
fdtd.html:
Yee FDTD: vacuum modes, dielectric interfaces and PML validation

Revision r2 adds a dielectric interface and left/right x-directed PML to the original two vacuum cases. The first part covers vacuum analytic modes; the extension covers normal-incidence Fresnel comparisons and boundary reflections of normal/oblique packets. The original code edition, figures and measurements are retained.

This original educational implementation evolves 2D TMz fields (Ez, Hx, Hy) with original vacuum cases in dimensionless homogeneous vacuum without current or charge sources. The original periodic plane waves and rectangular perfect-electric-conductor (PEC) cavity are compared with continuum analytic solutions. Grid refinement, numerical dispersion, a discrete invariant and an approximation to physical energy are measured separately.

Model, units and scope

∂tEz=∂xHy−∂yHx,∂tHx=−∂yEz,∂tHy=∂xEz,ϵ=μ=c=1.\partial_t E_z=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x,\qquad \partial_tH_x=-\partial_yE_z,\qquad \partial_tH_y=\partial_xE_z,\quad \epsilon=\mu=c=1.∂t​Ez​=∂x​Hy​−∂y​Hx​,∂t​Hx​=−∂y​Ez​,∂t​Hy​=∂x​Ez​,ϵ=μ=c=1.

Length, time and fields are normalized so ε=μ=c=1. The rectangle has Lx=1 and Ly=1.5, with mode indices (m,l)=(1,1). An oblique periodic mode on a rectangular domain exercises both spatial derivatives and magnetic-field signs. Dispersive media, losses, dielectric interfaces and driven sources are outside this edition.

Yee placement and staggered time update

Hx,i,j+1/2n+1/2=Hx,i,j+1/2n−1/2−ΔtΔy(Ei,j+1n−Ei,jn),Hy,i+1/2,jn+1/2=Hy,i+1/2,jn−1/2+ΔtΔx(Ei+1,jn−Ei,jn),Ei,jn+1=Ei,jn+Δt(Hy,i+1/2,jn+1/2−Hy,i−1/2,jn+1/2Δx−Hx,i,j+1/2n+1/2−Hx,i,j−1/2n+1/2Δy).\begin{aligned}H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n+1/2}&=H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n-1/2}-\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta y}(E_{i,j+1}^{n}-E_{i,j}^{n}),\\H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n+1/2}&=H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n-1/2}+\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}(E_{i+1,j}^{n}-E_{i,j}^{n}),\\E_{i,j}^{n+1}&=E_{i,j}^{n}+\Delta t\left(\frac{H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n+1/2}-H_{y,i-1/2,j}^{n+1/2}}{\Delta x}-\frac{H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n+1/2}-H_{x,i,j-1/2}^{n+1/2}}{\Delta y}\right).\end{aligned}Hx,i,j+1/2n+1/2​Hy,i+1/2,jn+1/2​Ei,jn+1​​=Hx,i,j+1/2n−1/2​−ΔyΔt​(Ei,j+1n​−Ei,jn​),=Hy,i+1/2,jn−1/2​+ΔxΔt​(Ei+1,jn​−Ei,jn​),=Ei,jn​+Δt​ΔxHy,i+1/2,jn+1/2​−Hy,i−1/2,jn+1/2​​−ΔyHx,i,j+1/2n+1/2​−Hx,i,j−1/2n+1/2​​​.​

Ez lives at nodes and integer times; Hx is displaced by half a y cell and Hy by half an x cell, both at half-integer times. Each step advances H first and then E. Initial E at time zero and H at −Δt/2 are sampled from analytic fields; assigning both fields time zero would introduce a first-order initialization error.

Periodic arrays omit duplicate endpoints and wrap differences. PEC walls fix tangential Ez=0 and update only interior electric nodes. Half weights for boundary magnetic samples make the weighted inner products compatible with discrete summation by parts and the energy identity.

Continuum periodic plane wave

kx=2πm/Lx,ky=2πl/Ly,ω=kx2+ky2,ϕ=kxx+kyy−ωt,Ez=cos⁡ϕ,Hx=(ky/ω)cos⁡ϕ,Hy=−(kx/ω)cos⁡ϕ.\begin{gathered}k_x=2\pi m/L_x,\quad k_y=2\pi l/L_y,\quad\omega=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2},\quad\phi=k_xx+k_yy-\omega t,\\ E_z=\cos\phi,\quad H_x=(k_y/\omega)\cos\phi,\quad H_y=-(k_x/\omega)\cos\phi.\end{gathered}kx​=2πm/Lx​,ky​=2πl/Ly​,ω=kx2​+ky2​​,ϕ=kx​x+ky​y−ωt,Ez​=cosϕ,Hx​=(ky​/ω)cosϕ,Hy​=−(kx​/ω)cosϕ.​

Evaluate the electric and both magnetic fields at their own spatial locations and times. Frequency supplies a phase-speed error separate from field error. A sampled continuum magnetic field need not have exactly zero discrete divergence, so the continuum-initialized run checks preservation of its initial divergence.

Continuum PEC cavity eigenmode

kx=mπ/Lx,ky=lπ/Ly,ω=kx2+ky2,Ez=sin⁡(kxx)sin⁡(kyy)cos⁡(ωt),Hx=−kyωsin⁡(kxx)cos⁡(kyy)sin⁡(ωt),Hy=kxωcos⁡(kxx)sin⁡(kyy)sin⁡(ωt).\begin{gathered}k_x=m\pi/L_x,\quad k_y=l\pi/L_y,\quad\omega=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2},\\E_z=\sin(k_xx)\sin(k_yy)\cos(\omega t),\\H_x=-\frac{k_y}{\omega}\sin(k_xx)\cos(k_yy)\sin(\omega t),\quad H_y=\frac{k_x}{\omega}\cos(k_xx)\sin(k_yy)\sin(\omega t).\end{gathered}kx​=mπ/Lx​,ky​=lπ/Ly​,ω=kx2​+ky2​​,Ez​=sin(kx​x)sin(ky​y)cos(ωt),Hx​=−ωky​​sin(kx​x)cos(ky​y)sin(ωt),Hy​=ωkx​​cos(kx​x)sin(ky​y)sin(ωt).​

This standing wave has Ez=0 on all four walls. It uses a different boundary implementation from the periodic wave, with checks of maximum wall electric field, eigenfrequency and field error. The cavity here is a z-invariant two-dimensional section; it does not cover the full three-dimensional cavity spectrum.

CFL condition and discrete dispersion

sin⁡2(ωhΔt/2)Δt2=sin⁡2(kxΔx/2)Δx2+sin⁡2(kyΔy/2)Δy2,S=ΔtΔx−2+Δy−2<1.\frac{\sin^2(\omega_h\Delta t/2)}{\Delta t^2}=\frac{\sin^2(k_x\Delta x/2)}{\Delta x^2}+\frac{\sin^2(k_y\Delta y/2)}{\Delta y^2},\qquad S=\Delta t\sqrt{\Delta x^{-2}+\Delta y^{-2}}<1.Δt2sin2(ωh​Δt/2)​=Δx2sin2(kx​Δx/2)​+Δy2sin2(ky​Δy/2)​,S=ΔtΔx−2+Δy−2​<1.

The fixed input sets a Courant-number ceiling of 0.7; S≥1 is rejected. Rounding the required step count upward and choosing Δt from that count reaches the prescribed 1.1-period comparison time exactly, with actual S at or slightly below 0.7. Refining the grid also refines the time step, so measured orders describe coupled spatial and temporal refinement. They are not separate experimental estimates of spatial order and temporal order.

A three-time-level recurrence for evolved modal projection coefficients measures frequency. Its convergence toward continuum ω is separate from agreement with discrete ωh. Additional tests initialize magnetic amplitudes with the discrete wave numbers and check the exact discrete eigenmode to roundoff accuracy.

Discrete invariant versus physical energy

U∗n=12∥En∥h2+12⟨Hn−1/2,Hn+1/2⟩h=constant,Hˉn=(Hn−1/2+Hn+1/2)/2,Usyncn=12(∥En∥h2+∥Hˉn∥h2),U∗n=Usyncn−Δt28∥curl⁡hEn∥h2.\begin{aligned}U_*^n&=\frac12\lVert E^n\rVert_h^2+\frac12\langle H^{n-1/2},H^{n+1/2}\rangle_h=\mathrm{constant},\\\bar H^n&=(H^{n-1/2}+H^{n+1/2})/2,\\ U_{\rm sync}^n&=\tfrac12(\lVert E^n\rVert_h^2+\lVert\bar H^n\rVert_h^2),\\ U_*^n&=U_{\rm sync}^n-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\lVert\operatorname{curl}_h E^n\rVert_h^2.\end{aligned}U∗n​HˉnUsyncn​U∗n​​=21​∥En∥h2​+21​⟨Hn−1/2,Hn+1/2⟩h​=constant,=(Hn−1/2+Hn+1/2)/2,=21​(∥En∥h2​+∥Hˉn∥h2​),=Usyncn​−8Δt2​∥curlh​En∥h2​.​

Inner products include cell area and the appropriate PEC boundary weights. U*, containing magnetic fields from two different half times, is conserved up to roundoff in the closed periodic/PEC systems. The strict CFL inequality also ensures positivity of this modified energy. Usync, using magnetic fields averaged to an integer time, is a second-order approximation to physical energy but is not exactly invariant.

For unit-amplitude continuum fields the total energies are LxLy/2 for the traveling periodic wave and LxLy/8 for the cavity standing wave. Twelve periods are used to track relative U* drift and the variation of Usync; the error against the analytic physical energy must decrease at approximately second order under grid/time refinement. Tests also check U* conservation with compatible random fields, beyond single eigenmodes.

Fixed inputs and measured results

eh=(∥Eh−E∥h2+∥Hh−H∥h2N2)1/2,p=log⁡(eh/eh/2)log⁡2.e_h=\left(\frac{\lVert E_h-E\rVert_h^2+\lVert H_h-H\rVert_h^2}{\mathcal N^2}\right)^{1/2},\qquad p=\frac{\log(e_h/e_{h/2})}{\log 2}.eh​=(N2∥Eh​−E∥h2​+∥Hh​−H∥h2​​)1/2,p=log2log(eh​/eh/2​)​.

Grids are 16×24, 32×48 and 64×96. Continuum field errors are evaluated exactly at the prescribed 1.1-period target, reached by adjusting the time step to an integer step count. H is compared at its actual half step before E. The combined-field denominator 𝒩² is the constant continuum modal norm (LxLy for the periodic wave, LxLy/4 for the cavity). Separate electric and magnetic errors are retained in JSON.

A Gaussian packet is normally incident on a flat interface between nonmagnetic, lossless, nondispersive media ε₁=1 and ε₂=4, μ=1. The interface x=8 coincides with an electric node, assigned the arithmetic mean permittivity. This is a y-invariant reduction of 2D TMz. Analytic values are r=−1/3, t=2/3, R=1/9 and T=8/9.

The domain is 16×1, initial center x=4, width 0.5, comparison time t=8, with 160/320/640 x cells and 4 y cells. Incident, reflected and transmitted packets have separate continuum formulas; electric amplitudes are measured by projection. Packet-energy R,T are integrated using ε|E|² and magnetic fields, separately from simply squaring amplitudes. The shared interface-node quadrature weight is split between left and right regions.

pic.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
pic.html:
Particle-in-cell / PIC

Plasma PIC represents a distribution by computational particles and self-consistent fields by a mesh. Its smoothing, collisionality and sampling error differ from direct all-pairs Coulomb dynamics.

Problem and representative equations

Start with nonrelativistic electrostatic Vlasov–Poisson. Computational particle p has weight wₚ, charge qₚ and position xₚ. Dimensionless shape weights Sᵢ sum to one, and Vᵢ is cell volume. Deposit ρ, solve Poisson with the stated boundary conditions, and use E=−∇φ.

ρi=1Vi∑pwpqpSi(xp),−∇h2ϕi=ρi/ϵ0,v˙p=(qp/mp)Eh(xp).\rho_i=\frac1{V_i}\sum_p w_pq_pS_i(\mathbf x_p),\qquad -\nabla_h^2\phi_i=\rho_i/\epsilon_0,\qquad \dot{\mathbf v}_p=(q_p/m_p)\mathbf E_h(\mathbf x_p).ρi​=Vi​1​p∑​wp​qp​Si​(xp​),−∇h2​ϕi​=ρi​/ϵ0​,v˙p​=(qp​/mp​)Eh​(xp​).

Algorithm

Repeat charge deposition, field solution, particle gathering and particle pushing; include background ions in ρ. Electromagnetic PIC additionally needs current deposition and Maxwell updates consistent with discrete continuity. Dawson’s sheet model is a historical particle-plasma example, not the definition of every PIC discretization.

Conditions and pitfalls

Explicit electrostatic PIC must examine plasma-frequency time scales and Debye-length resolution. Exact restrictions depend on the particle pusher, shape and field solver. Separate sampling convergence in particle count from grid/time convergence, and check self-force and finite-grid heating.

What to check

Begin with single-particle self-force, a uniform neutral distribution, and small-amplitude plasma oscillations or Landau damping. Report charge, energy drift, particle-count dependence and independent random realizations. Compare damping rates only within the linear-amplitude regime used by the theory.

amg.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
amg.html:
Algebraic multigrid / AMG

AMG constructs a multilevel hierarchy and interpolation from a matrix. Smooth error means error that relaxation removes poorly, rather than only geometrically long-wavelength error.

Problem and representative equations

For Au=b, use residual r=b−Au, restriction R and interpolation P. The Galerkin coarse operator is A_c=RAP. Correct the fine approximation using a coarse residual solve. The inverse in the formula expresses the principle; a multilevel cycle normally approximates that solve recursively.

Ac=RAP,r=b−Au,u←u+PAc−1Rr.A_c=RAP,\qquad r=b-Au,\qquad u\leftarrow u+P A_c^{-1}Rr.Ac​=RAP,r=b−Au,u←u+PAc−1​Rr.

Algorithm

A cycle applies pre-relaxation, computes/restricts the residual, corrects on the coarse space and post-relaxes. Classical AMG uses strength connections and C/F splitting; aggregation variants group unknowns. Near-nullspace information, such as rigid motions for elasticity, must be represented by interpolation.

Conditions and pitfalls

Success on a scalar elliptic problem does not ensure robustness for nonsymmetric advection, saddle points or strong anisotropy. CG preconditioning requires compatible symmetry/positive-definiteness properties. A pure-Neumann problem still has a constant nullspace and a right-hand-side compatibility condition.

What to check

Use manufactured Poisson solutions while varying mesh size and coefficient contrast. Measure true residuals, solution errors and per-cycle reduction; record hierarchy sizes and nonzero counts. Few iterations do not establish small discretization error.

qr-svd.title: QR, SVD and least squares
qr-svd.html:
QR, SVD and least squares

Least squares, low-rank approximation and conditioning call for different matrix decompositions. QR reduces a problem to orthogonal transformations and a triangular solve; SVD exposes singular values and resolvable directions.

Problem and representative equations

For a real m×n matrix with m≥n, thin QR has QᵀQ=I and upper triangular R. Full column rank gives the least-squares solve Rx=Qᵀb. SVD has nonnegative singular values σᵢ. Truncating small σᵢ in a pseudoinverse regularizes the problem and can change the solution being sought.

A=QR=UΣVT,min⁡x∥Ax−b∥2,A+b=∑σi>τuiTbσivi(truncated).A=QR=U\Sigma V^T,\qquad \min_x\|Ax-b\|_2,\qquad A^+b=\sum_{\sigma_i>\tau}\frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}v_i\quad\text{(truncated)}.A=QR=UΣVT,xmin​∥Ax−b∥2​,A+b=σi​>τ∑​σi​uiT​b​vi​(truncated).

Algorithm

Householder QR eliminates subdiagonal entries with reflections and generally maintains orthogonality better than classical Gram–Schmidt. Consider column pivoting or SVD for rank diagnosis. Classical SVD algorithms reduce to bidiagonal form using orthogonal transformations rather than explicitly forming normal equations.

Conditions and pitfalls

For full column rank, κ₂(AᵀA)=κ₂(A)². A small residual can coexist with uncertain coefficients under ill-conditioning or noise. Choose a numerical-rank threshold relative to scale, rounding and measurement uncertainty, and consider column scaling when variables have different units.

What to check

Check relative factorization residuals, orthogonality and Aᵀ(Ax−b). Test prescribed singular values and rank-deficient cases, and compare solution changes under controlled data perturbations.

eigensolvers.title: Krylov eigenvalue solvers
eigensolvers.html:
Krylov eigenvalue solvers

Krylov eigensolvers approximate a few eigenpairs through a small subspace instead of diagonalizing a large matrix in full. Arnoldi, symmetric Lanczos and shift-invert require different assumptions.

Problem and representative equations

Build Kₘ(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Aᵐ⁻¹v}. Arnoldi gives an orthonormal Vₘ and upper-Hessenberg Hₘ. Solve Hₘy=θy and set x=Vₘy. The last Arnoldi vector and hₘ₊₁,ₘ give the Ritz residual.

AVm=VmHm+hm+1,mvm+1emT,∥Ax−θx∥2=∣hm+1,memTy∣(∥y∥2=1).AV_m=V_mH_m+h_{m+1,m}v_{m+1}e_m^T,\qquad \|Ax-\theta x\|_2=|h_{m+1,m}e_m^Ty|\quad(\|y\|_2=1).AVm​=Vm​Hm​+hm+1,m​vm+1​emT​,∥Ax−θx∥2​=∣hm+1,m​emT​y∣(∥y∥2​=1).

Algorithm

Expand the basis using matrix-vector products and orthogonalization, solve the projected eigenproblem and restart when needed. Hermitian matrices permit a Lanczos three-term recurrence. Shift-invert targets interior eigenvalues but each inverse action requires a linear solve.

Conditions and pitfalls

Finite-precision loss of orthogonality can create ghost duplicates. For nonnormal matrices, a small residual need not imply a comparably small eigenvalue error. State B and the inner product in generalized problems Ax=λBx, and assess inner-solve tolerances for shift-invert.

What to check

Check scaled residuals ∥Ax−θx∥/(∥A∥+|θ|), orthogonality, known eigenpairs and clustered/repeated eigenvalues. For symmetric cases compare Rayleigh quotients, and record restarts and initial-vector sensitivity.

splines.title: Spline interpolation
splines.html:
Spline interpolation

Splines join piecewise low-degree polynomials with specified continuity. Distinguish them from a single global high-degree polynomial and distinguish exact interpolation from smoothing noisy data.

Problem and representative equations

Use a nondecreasing knot sequence tᵢ and degree p. Nᵢ,₀ is the indicator of [tᵢ,tᵢ₊₁); zero-denominator terms in the recursion are defined as zero. Degree p means order p+1.

Algorithm

Represent s=ΣcᵢNᵢ,ₚ and determine coefficients by interpolation or least squares. A natural cubic spline sets endpoint second derivatives to zero; clamped conditions prescribe endpoint first derivatives. Determining coefficients and evaluating the spline by de Boor’s algorithm are separate stages.

Conditions and pitfalls

An interior knot of multiplicity r generally gives Cᵖ⁻ʳ continuity. Cubic splines do not automatically preserve monotonicity or positivity and can overshoot. Extrapolation depends on the chosen endpoint convention and is not covered by an in-interval interpolation argument.

What to check

Check polynomial reproduction, one-sided derivatives at knots and endpoint conditions. For noiseless functions study refinement; for noisy data separately report held-out prediction errors and smoothing-parameter dependence.

quadrature.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
quadrature.html:
Gaussian and adaptive quadrature

Gaussian quadrature selects nodes and weights for a measure to integrate polynomials efficiently. Adaptive integration separately allocates function evaluations using local error estimates.

Problem and representative equations

For a positive measure, an n-point Gaussian rule is exact through degree 2n−1 when the required moments exist. The Jacobi matrix J of orthogonal-polynomial recurrence coefficients has quadrature nodes as eigenvalues. Weights are μ₀ times squared first components of normalized eigenvectors, with μ₀=∫w.

∫abf(x)w(x) dx≈∑j=1nωjf(xj),Jvj=xjvj,ωj=μ0(vj)12.\int_a^b f(x)w(x)\,dx\approx\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_jf(x_j),\qquad Jv_j=x_jv_j,\quad\omega_j=\mu_0(v_j)_1^2.∫ab​f(x)w(x)dx≈j=1∑n​ωj​f(xj​),Jvj​=xj​vj​,ωj​=μ0​(vj​)12​.

Algorithm

Golub–Welsch solves this symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem. Adaptive Gauss–Kronrod-type integration uses differences between nested rules to estimate local errors, subdivides intervals and checks absolute/relative tolerances. The rule difference is not an unconditional error bound.

Conditions and pitfalls

Singularities, jumps, rapid oscillations and narrow peaks can be missed by sampled nodes. Split at known discontinuities and consider transformations or matched weighted rules. Relative tolerance alone is unsuitable when the integral is close to zero.

What to check

Verify degree of exactness on monomials, then test nonpolynomials with known integrals, singularities and narrow peaks. Record estimated versus true error, evaluation count and termination caused by subdivision limits.

chebyshev.title: Chebyshev approximation
chebyshev.html:
Chebyshev approximation

Chebyshev approximation uses endpoint-clustered nodes and a connection with trigonometric functions. Interpolation, weighted projection and best uniform approximation are distinct constructions.

Problem and representative equations

Set Tₖ(cosθ)=cos(kθ) and approximate f on [−1,1] by ΣaₖTₖ. Lobatto nodes xⱼ=cos(jπ/n) allow interpolation coefficients to be computed by a discrete cosine transform. Orthogonality uses weight (1−x²)⁻¹/², not the unit weight of Legendre polynomials.

T0(x)=1,T1(x)=x,Tk+1(x)=2xTk(x)−Tk−1(x),xj=cos⁡(jπ/n).T_0(x)=1,\quad T_1(x)=x,\quad T_{k+1}(x)=2xT_k(x)-T_{k-1}(x),\qquad x_j=\cos(j\pi/n).T0​(x)=1,T1​(x)=x,Tk+1​(x)=2xTk​(x)−Tk−1​(x),xj​=cos(jπ/n).

Algorithm

Map the physical interval, sample the nodes, compute coefficients and evaluate the series by recurrence. Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature integrates the interpolant; its nodes and exactness properties are not identical to Gaussian quadrature.

Conditions and pitfalls

Analytic functions can give rapid coefficient decay, while jumps cause Gibbs oscillations and finite smoothness slows decay. Differentiation amplifies coefficient errors. A small coefficient tail alone cannot rule out unresolved features between sampling nodes.

What to check

Test reproduction of Tₖ, nodal interpolation and approximation of exp(x), then compare convergence for an absolute value or jump. Measure errors off the interpolation grid and verify derivative scaling under interval maps.

wavelets.title: Wavelets
wavelets.html:
Wavelets

Wavelets resolve structure in both location and scale. Compared with global Fourier modes, they describe localized changes through a hierarchy of resolutions.

Problem and representative equations

An orthonormal discrete wavelet system expands a function in coarse scaling coefficients c and detail coefficients d. The factor 2ʲ/² preserves the L2 norm of ψⱼ,ₖ. The stated energy identity assumes a complete orthonormal system and compatible boundary treatment.

f=∑kcJ,kϕJ,k+∑j≥J∑kdj,kψj,k,∥f∥22=∑k∣cJ,k∣2+∑j≥J,k∣dj,k∣2.f=\sum_kc_{J,k}\phi_{J,k}+\sum_{j\ge J}\sum_kd_{j,k}\psi_{j,k},\qquad\|f\|_2^2=\sum_k|c_{J,k}|^2+\sum_{j\ge J,k}|d_{j,k}|^2.f=k∑​cJ,k​ϕJ,k​+j≥J∑​k∑​dj,k​ψj,k​,∥f∥22​=k∑​∣cJ,k​∣2+j≥J,k∑​∣dj,k​∣2.

Algorithm

Mallat’s multiresolution algorithm filters and downsamples into coarse and detail coefficients, then recurses on the coarse part. Matched synthesis filters reconstruct the signal. More vanishing moments can sparsify smooth components but affect support width and boundary handling.

Conditions and pitfalls

On finite intervals specify periodic/symmetric extensions or boundary wavelets. Coefficient thresholding loses information and does not automatically preserve conservation laws or shock positivity. Distinguish continuous transforms, orthonormal discrete transforms and biorthogonal energy relations.

What to check

Check reconstruction, Parseval energy and vanishing moments on low-degree polynomials. Vary thresholds and report retained coefficients, L2/maximum errors and boundary artifacts.

optimization.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
optimization.html:
Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization

Gradient methods use first derivatives; quasi-Newton methods infer curvature from gradient differences. This introduction treats smooth unconstrained minimization, separately from constrained optimality conditions.

Problem and representative equations

Let gₖ=∇f(xₖ), Hₖ approximate the inverse Hessian and pₖ=−Hₖgₖ. In BFGS, s=xₖ₊₁−xₖ, y=gₖ₊₁−gₖ and ρ=1/(yᵀs). Hₖ=I gives steepest descent in the chosen coordinates, so units and scaling matter.

xk+1=xk−αkHkgk,Hk+1=(I−ρsyT)Hk(I−ρysT)+ρssT.x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_kg_k,\qquad H_{k+1}=(I-\rho sy^T)H_k(I-\rho ys^T)+\rho ss^T.xk+1​=xk​−αk​Hk​gk​,Hk+1​=(I−ρsyT)Hk​(I−ρysT)+ρssT.

Algorithm

Evaluate gradients, select a step length using a line search and update curvature. BFGS enforces Hₖ₊₁y=s with a symmetric update. Positive-definite Hₖ and yᵀs>0 preserve positive definiteness. Poor curvature requires an explicit policy such as skipping or damping the update.

Conditions and pitfalls

For nonconvex problems, finding a local stationary point is different from finding a global optimum. Noisy gradients, nonsmooth objectives and inaccurate inner PDE solves can corrupt curvature. Do not stop on relative objective change alone: inspect gradient norms, step sizes, limits and termination reasons.

What to check

Vary conditioning on positive-definite quadratics with known minima and check gradients by directional differences. On curved valleys vary initialization, scaling and line searches. Decreasing an objective does not validate physical assumptions or constraints.

Verified implementation example: adjoint-gradient fitting of the Bratu synthetic inverse problem

Next: two-coefficient Bratu fitting, regularization and identifiability — The existing general-method sections remain; the dedicated chapter contains the two-coefficient execution checks.

Publication scope and related entries

This page gives general gradient/quasi-Newton reading. Implemented scope is the separate Bratu synthetic inverse example: a scalar box-constrained projected-gradient method with Armijo backtracking. BFGS, general quasi-Newton methods and the broader checks proposed on this page are not implemented or verified by that example.

monte-carlo.title: Monte Carlo integration
monte-carlo.html:
Monte Carlo integration

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral as an expectation. Accuracy depends on the sampling distribution, weights and variance, not merely on using random numbers.

Problem and representative equations

Draw independent samples Xᵢ from a density p covering the support of f and average Yᵢ=f(Xᵢ)/p(Xᵢ). With finite second moment, estimate standard error by s_Y/√N. Uniform sampling requires the domain-volume factor.

I=∫f(x) dx=Ep ⁣[f(X)p(X)],I^N=1N∑i=1Nf(Xi)p(Xi),SE⁡^=sY/N.I=\int f(x)\,dx=\mathbb E_p\!\left[\frac{f(X)}{p(X)}\right],\qquad \widehat I_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{f(X_i)}{p(X_i)},\quad\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=s_Y/\sqrt N.I=∫f(x)dx=Ep​[p(X)f(X)​],IN​=N1​i=1∑N​p(Xi​)f(Xi​)​,SE=sY​/N​.

Algorithm

Specify the distribution and random generator, draw samples and compute the weighted mean and variance. Importance sampling concentrates p where contributions matter, while monitoring heavy tails of f/p. Record generator/version, seed and sample count for reproducibility.

Conditions and pitfalls

The N⁻¹/² scale is statistical and conditional on assumptions such as independence and finite variance; it is not a deterministic bound for each run. Rare events and missed peaks can make variance estimates misleading. Correlated MCMC samples need a different uncertainty calculation.

What to check

Use repeated independent runs on known integrals to examine N scaling and interval coverage. Record actual mean error separately from estimated uncertainty, and verify that changes in importance density preserve the target integral.

Publication scope and related entries

Integrate x² under U[0,1]. Compare 256 independent seeds with analytic integral and variance, checking N^-1/2 RMS scaling and interval coverage. Excludes MCMC and rare events. Inputs, code, measured values and tolerances are linked from the method and execution pages. Not every general verification proposal above has been executed.

mcmc.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
mcmc.html:
Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC

MCMC constructs a Markov chain with a chosen invariant distribution when direct independent sampling is difficult. Invariance and adequate exploration in a finite run are separate requirements.

Problem and representative equations

For an unnormalized target π and proposal q(y|x), use the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability. Unknown target normalization cancels. Proposal factors cancel only for symmetric proposals; omitting them for an asymmetric proposal changes the target.

a(x,y)=min⁡ ⁣(1,π(y)q(x∣y)π(x)q(y∣x)),Neff≈N1+2∑k≥1ρk.a(x,y)=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right),\qquad N_{\rm eff}\approx\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}.a(x,y)=min(1,π(x)q(y∣x)π(y)q(x∣y)​),Neff​≈1+2∑k≥1​ρk​N​.

Algorithm

Propose y, accept or retain x, and keep rejected repetitions as samples. Assess initial transients and use dispersed initial states across chains. Interpret autocorrelation-based effective sample size only when stationarity and autocorrelation estimation are credible.

Conditions and pitfalls

Detailed balance alone does not establish irreducibility or aperiodicity. Multimodality, correlations and boundaries can slow mixing. High acceptance can simply reflect tiny moves. Thinning is not a general way to increase information for a fixed computational budget.

What to check

Check means, variances and quantiles for known targets, including asymmetric proposals and rejections. For multimodal cases report between-chain comparisons, autocorrelations, effective sample sizes and uncertainty; visually flat traces alone are not proof of convergence.

sde.title: Stochastic differential equations
sde.html:
Stochastic differential equations

Brownian increments in an SDE scale as √Δt. Adding random numbers to an ODE solver does not by itself specify the stochastic interpretation or convergence order.

Problem and representative equations

The formula uses a scalar Itô SDE. a is drift, b is diffusion and ΔWₙ are independent Gaussian increments with mean zero and variance Δt. Euler–Maruyama evaluates both coefficients at n. Converting a Stratonovich equation requires the appropriate drift correction.

dX=a(X,t) dt+b(X,t) dW,Xn+1=Xn+a(Xn,tn)Δt+b(Xn,tn)ΔWn.dX=a(X,t)\,dt+b(X,t)\,dW,\qquad X_{n+1}=X_n+a(X_n,t_n)\Delta t+b(X_n,t_n)\Delta W_n.dX=a(X,t)dt+b(X,t)dW,Xn+1​=Xn​+a(Xn​,tn​)Δt+b(Xn​,tn​)ΔWn​.

Algorithm

Generate Wiener increments and advance deterministic and stochastic terms. Strong-error refinement must couple paths by summing fine increments into the coarse increment. Weak error concerns expectations of test functions, not the discrepancy of one pair of paths.

Conditions and pitfalls

Under suitable global Lipschitz, moment and smoothness assumptions, Euler–Maruyama typically has strong order 1/2 and weak order 1. Superlinear growth or positivity constraints can invalidate the method and require specialized treatments. Sampling uncertainty may dominate weak discretization error.

What to check

Use geometric Brownian exact paths and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck moments to test strong and weak convergence separately. Record step size, random streams, sample count and uncertainty, including negative states or boundary violations.

Publication scope and related entries

Euler–Maruyama for scalar geometric Brownian motion. Coarse/fine steps and analytic endpoints share the same Brownian paths; measure strong RMS error across 4096 paths. Does not validate general SDEs, MCMC or weak convergence order. Inputs, code, measured values and tolerances are linked from the method and execution pages. Not every general verification proposal above has been executed.

adjoint.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
adjoint.html:
Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity

Compute how a converged numerical solution responds to a changing coefficient. Implement implicit state sensitivities and a discrete adjoint gradient for Bratu’s equation, then check them against an exact continuous family, re-solved parameter differences and spatial refinement.

Differentiate the converged equation

Consider a state u defined by an equation depending on parameters θ rather than by an explicit formula. For n states and m parameters, denote residual partial derivatives by J and B. All gradients below are column vectors.

F(u(θ),θ)=0,J=Fu∈Rn×n,B=Fθ∈Rn×m.F(u(\theta),\theta)=0,\qquad J=F_u\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\qquad B=F_\theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}.F(u(θ),θ)=0,J=Fu​∈Rn×n,B=Fθ​∈Rn×m.

If F is continuously differentiable near the solution and J is nonsingular, the implicit function theorem defines a local derivative of the solution. Applying the chain rule gives a sensitivity equation. This does not establish global uniqueness or automatically select one branch among several roots.

Implicit differentiation: solve the sensitivity equation

JS+B=0,S=dudθ,Jsv=−Bv,sv=Sv.J S+B=0,\qquad S=\frac{du}{d\theta},\qquad J s_v=-Bv,\qquad s_v=S v.JS+B=0,S=dθdu​,Jsv​=−Bv,sv​=Sv.

S is the state Jacobian with respect to all parameters. If only one direction v is needed, solve one linear system with right-hand side −Bv. Do not explicitly form an inverse of J. Analytic expressions, AD or appropriately checked finite differences can supply J and B.

The example first solves the primal problem using the existing Newton method, then assembles residual partial derivatives at the computed state. AD evaluates local derivatives of the residual. The implementation does not differentiate an unrolled finite sequence of Newton iterations.

Discrete adjoints: obtain an objective gradient

Observation fitting and design often need the total derivative of a scalar objective rather than every state sensitivity. Separate the partial derivative r at fixed state from the contribution Sᵀq due to the changing state.

L^(θ)=L(u(θ),θ),q=∇uL,r=∇θL,∇θL^=r+STq.\widehat L(\theta)=L(u(\theta),\theta),\qquad q=\nabla_uL,\quad r=\nabla_\theta L,\qquad \nabla_\theta\widehat L=r+S^Tq.L(θ)=L(u(θ),θ),q=∇u​L,r=∇θ​L,∇θ​L=r+STq.

Solving a transpose system gives the same gradient without storing every column of S. The Lagrangian convention used here subtracts the residual term, so the term involving B has a minus sign.

JTp=q,∇θL^=r−BTp.J^Tp=q,\qquad \boxed{\nabla_\theta\widehat L=r-B^Tp}.JTp=q,∇θ​L=r−BTp​.
L(u,θ,p)=L(u,θ)−pTF(u,θ),∇uL=q−JTp=0.\mathcal L(u,\theta,p)=L(u,\theta)-p^TF(u,\theta),\qquad \nabla_u\mathcal L=q-J^Tp=0.L(u,θ,p)=L(u,θ)−pTF(u,θ),∇u​L=q−JTp=0.

With many parameters and few objectives, adjoint solves per objective can replace sensitivity solves per parameter. Factorizations can be shared across right-hand sides, and a VJP can evaluate Bᵀp. This one-parameter, one-objective example has one right-hand side for either method and makes no speed claim. The implementation assembles and solves small dense matrices.

The same Bratu discretization and branch

Use the same Bratu equation on [0,1] with zero Dirichlet data as in the AD chapter. Here n counts interior unknowns. Coordinates, state, parameter and objective are dimensionless in this educational model. The grid and boundary data are independent of the parameter.

The continuous problem has an exact family parameterized by α. The point α=1 uses the same parameter as the earlier Bratu example. The verification uses α=1 and 2, both corresponding to the smaller-solution branch reached from zero initial data.

Retain the objective’s explicit parameter dependence

Lh(u,λ)=h2∑i=1nui2+β2λ2,β=0.05,q=hu,r=βλ.L_h(u,\lambda)=\frac h2\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i^2+\frac\beta2\lambda^2,\qquad \beta=0.05,\qquad q=h u,\quad r=\beta\lambda.Lh​(u,λ)=2h​i=1∑n​ui2​+2β​λ2,β=0.05,q=hu,r=βλ.

The first term is a trapezoidal approximation of the integral of half the squared state. Zero endpoint values leave only interior contributions. The second term deliberately retains explicit parameter dependence, so dropping βλ can be detected separately from the state-mediated contribution. This is a defined derivative-check objective, not a fit to observational data.

JTp=hu,gdirect=βλ+huTs,gadjoint=βλ+pTeu.J^Tp=h u,\qquad g_{\mathrm{direct}}=\beta\lambda+h u^T s,\qquad g_{\mathrm{adjoint}}=\beta\lambda+p^T e^u.JTp=hu,gdirect​=βλ+huTs,gadjoint​=βλ+pTeu.

Here p is a discrete adjoint in the Euclidean inner product; the quadrature weight h is included in q=h u. Do not identify p directly with nodal values of a continuous PDE adjoint defined in an L² inner product. Nonuniform grids, finite elements and parameter-dependent quadrature require consistent treatment of mass matrices and weights.

Verification: separate sensitivities, gradients and spatial error

The saved measurements and source hashes record controls, tested points, residuals and errors.

  1. Residual partial derivatives. Treat state and parameter as independent inputs; compare AD evaluations of J and F_λ with analytic expressions. A parameter-only seed holds u fixed.
  2. Sensitivity and adjoint equations. Use the same converged state and recompute each linear-system residual. Compare direct and adjoint gradients, including the explicit βλ term.
  3. Parameter differences. Solve the nonlinear problem again at λ+ε and λ−ε before differencing the objective. Perturbing λ while holding the state fixed does not test the total derivative.
  4. Spatial refinement. For n=15, 31 and 63 compare discrete sensitivity with the exact continuous s_* in the maximum nodal norm. Direct–adjoint agreement alone does not establish spatial accuracy.

Saved measurements. The points α=1 and 2 have λ≈1.5728955 and 3.3597947. All six regular cases start at zero with an absolute primal residual Euclidean tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰ and at most 40 updates. Direct and adjoint gradients differ by less than 1.4×10⁻¹⁵. Primal residuals are at most 5.3×10⁻¹¹; the relative sensitivity and adjoint residuals defined below are at most 2.3×10⁻¹³ and 1.9×10⁻¹³, respectively.

For n=15, 31 and 63, maximum nodal sensitivity errors are approximately 3.0015×10⁻⁴, 7.4860×10⁻⁵ and 1.8704×10⁻⁵ at α=1; at α=2 they are 2.6708×10⁻², 6.4898×10⁻³ and 1.6112×10⁻³. Halving h reduces errors by about four; the coarser α=2 grid shows a larger departure from the asymptotic regime. These are spatial sensitivity errors, not direct–adjoint discrepancies.

gFD(ε)=Lh(u(λ+ε),λ+ε)−Lh(u(λ−ε),λ−ε)2ε.g_{\mathrm{FD}}(\varepsilon)=\frac{L_h(u(\lambda+\varepsilon),\lambda+\varepsilon)-L_h(u(\lambda-\varepsilon),\lambda-\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}.gFD​(ε)=2εLh​(u(λ+ε),λ+ε)−Lh​(u(λ−ε),λ−ε)​.

The n=31 difference check uses 17 perturbations ε from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁹. In this saved run, agreement is good near ε=10⁻⁵, where the absolute gradient difference for α=2 is about 4.0×10⁻¹¹. At ε=10⁻⁹ it grows to about 1.3×10⁻⁶. Making perturbations ever smaller does not give an ever more accurate gradient.

The parameter perturbation ε and spatial mesh spacing h are different quantities. Sweep ε and vary the nonlinear solve tolerance to expose regimes dominated by truncation, incomplete convergence or roundoff. Finite differences provide an independent check, not a uniformly optimal reference at every perturbation.

The Bratu Jacobian here is symmetric, so replacing Jᵀ incorrectly by J would escape detection on this problem alone. A separate manufactured implicit system with a nonsymmetric matrix and multiple parameters therefore independently checks direct sensitivities and adjoint gradients. That test checks transposition, signs and shapes; it does not validate another physical model.

A separate α=2, n=31 sweep uses primal tolerances 10⁻², 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻¹⁰. At ε=10⁻⁴, absolute finite-difference gradient error decreases from about 3.2×10⁻⁵ for the loose 10⁻² solve to about 3.5×10⁻⁸ for the two tighter settings. The 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻¹⁰ controls accept the same Newton iterates, so their curves overlap. Do not interpret every tolerance tightening as a distinct result or a strict monotonic improvement.

Incomplete solves, conditioning and unrolled iterations

rF=∥F(u,λ)∥2,ρs=∥Js+Fλ∥2∥Fλ∥2,ρp=∥JTp−q∥2∥q∥2.r_F=\|F(u,\lambda)\|_2,\qquad \rho_s=\frac{\|Js+F_\lambda\|_2}{\|F_\lambda\|_2},\qquad \rho_p=\frac{\|J^Tp-q\|_2}{\|q\|_2}.rF​=∥F(u,λ)∥2​,ρs​=∥Fλ​∥2​∥Js+Fλ​∥2​​,ρp​=∥q∥2​∥JTp−q∥2​​.

Primal, sensitivity and adjoint equations have separate residuals. A small linear residual does not repair an unconverged state: derivatives are then evaluated at an approximate state rather than an exact root. An ill-conditioned J can amplify small primal errors into state or gradient errors. Conditioning also depends on scaling and grid size, so cross-grid condition numbers are not algorithm rankings.

Differentiating finitely many iterations gives the derivative of a map depending on the initial state and executed updates. Implicit differentiation targets the equations defining a local converged solution. State that distinction when differentiating through stopping criteria, line searches or adaptive decisions. A computed gradient alone establishes neither inverse-problem identifiability nor optimizer convergence.

Continuous sensitivities and applicability

−s′′−λeus=eu,s(0)=s(1)=0.-s^{\prime\prime}-\lambda e^u s=e^u,\qquad s(0)=s(1)=0.−s′′−λeus=eu,s(0)=s(1)=0.

Differentiating the continuous Bratu equation with respect to λ gives this boundary-value problem. Here centered differences also provide its natural discretization, and refinement can be checked against s_* from the exact family. In general, discretizing a continuous adjoint and differentiating a discrete residual need not agree on a finite mesh. Include parameter dependence of boundaries, grids, observation operators and quadrature weights.

Verified scope is a specified smooth steady Bratu branch and a small nonsymmetric manufactured system. It does not cover shocks, limiters, contacts/events, transient adjoints, singular bifurcation points or inverse fitting to real observations. Read discretization error, derivative implementation and physical-model validity separately.

A separate continuous reference is also provided for the objective gradient. Integrate the exact-family u_α and s_* and compare 96- and 192-point Gauss quadrature.

g∗=βλ+∫01uα(x)s∗(x) dx.g_* =\beta\lambda+\int_0^1 u_\alpha(x)s_*(x)\,dx.g∗​=βλ+∫01​uα​(x)s∗​(x)dx.

The references are about 0.1027083914 at α=1 and 0.5823748758 at α=2. The n=31 discrete adjoint gradients are about 0.1027218294 and 0.5857608186, respectively. Spatial error remains despite near-machine-precision direct–adjoint agreement. The two quadrature orders differ by less than 4.4×10⁻¹⁵ in both cases; their difference is a convergence diagnostic rather than a rigorous quadrature error bound.

Run and inspect the fixed release

Extract the dated release ZIP and follow its README in a new Python environment. The earlier AD supplement and other releases are not overwritten.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/build_bratu_sensitivity.py
python -m pytest tests/test_bratu_sensitivity.py

Inspect the sensitivity/adjoint source, figure and evidence builder, test source, file inventory and SHA-256 hashes, and independent-extraction verification record.

The existing AD foundation chapter explains how residual derivatives are obtained. Blondel et al. (2022), Section 2.1, and the official JAXopt references provide further discussion of root derivatives and their JVP/VJP constructions. This independent example uses NumPy and adds neither a JAX/JAXopt dependency nor a performance comparison with those libraries.

Automatic differentiation foundation · Newton and conditioning

The nine dedicated tests are rerun from an independently extracted copy of the release. The verification receipt also records checks of numerical evidence, the rebuilt figure and file hashes.

The fixed sensitivity release in this chapter does not fit observations. A separate follow-up uses its adjoint construction to estimate λ from synthetic observations. Bratu inverse problem: fit a parameter to synthetic observations

Next: two-coefficient Bratu fitting, regularization and identifiability — This chapter retains its dated supplement’s scope; the multi-parameter extension has a separate chapter and release.

Publication scope and related entries

An educational implementation verifies implicit state sensitivity and a discrete adjoint gradient on a specified smaller-solution Bratu branch, with a separate nonsymmetric multiparameter manufactured transpose test. State, derivative, mesh and parameter-perturbation errors are separated. Scope is small steady dense systems; it does not provide general reverse-mode AD, transient adjoints, singular-point continuation or a real-data inverse solver.

radiation-transport.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
radiation-transport.html:
Radiation transport and moment methods

Radiation transport resolves intensity in space, direction and frequency. Moment methods reduce the angular dimension but require closure for information removed by integration.

Problem and representative equations

Use frequency-integrated grey intensity I in a static medium, with isotropic emissivity η and absorption coefficient κ of inverse-length units; omit scattering here. Define E=(1/c)∫I dΩ, F=∫nI dΩ and P=(1/c)∫nnI dΩ. Moment equations for E and F require a prescription for P.

1c∂tI+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂tE+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂tF+∇⋅P=−κF/c. rac1c\partial_t I+\mathbf n\cdot abla I=\eta-\kappa I,\qquad\partial_t E+ abla\cdot\mathbf F=4\pi\eta-c\kappa E,\qquad c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf F+ abla\cdot\mathbf P=-\kappa\mathbf F/c.c1​∂t​I+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂t​E+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂t​F+∇⋅P=−κF/c.

Algorithm

Discrete ordinates discretizes angle directly; moment methods close P=D E. M1 obtains D locally from E and F, while flux-limited diffusion instead approximates F from the gradient of E. Check optically thick and free-streaming limits and couple matter exchange through a consistent energy balance.

Conditions and pitfalls

M1 generally cannot propagate crossing beams independently. FLD ties flux to the energy gradient, limiting shadows and strongly anisotropic fields. A reduced light speed changes transport/relaxation scales and must be justified against the physical time scales of interest.

What to check

Test exponential absorption, isotropic diffusion, free streaming/shadows and crossing beams separately. Check E≥0, |F|≤cE, matter-plus-radiation energy and angular/spatial/time convergence. Distinguish closure error from discretization error.

Publication scope and related entries

Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method.

dsmc.title: DSMC and kinetic transport
dsmc.html:
DSMC and kinetic transport

DSMC approximates dilute-gas Boltzmann collisions by stochastic collisions between computational particles. It differs from deterministic pair-potential molecular dynamics and from self-consistent plasma PIC fields.

Problem and representative equations

Consider Boltzmann f with molecular velocity v, acceleration a and collision operator Q. A simulator particle represents F_N physical molecules. In a cell of volume V_c, sample pair collisions according to total cross section σ_T and relative speed g. State the phase-space number-density normalization of f.

∂tf+v⋅∇xf+a⋅∇vf=Q(f,f),Ppair∼FNσTg ΔtVc.\partial_t f+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla_x f+\mathbf a\cdot\nabla_v f=Q(f,f),\qquad P_{\rm pair}\sim \frac{F_N\sigma_T g\,\Delta t}{V_c}.∂t​f+v⋅∇x​f+a⋅∇v​f=Q(f,f),Ppair​∼Vc​FN​σT​gΔt​.

Algorithm

Move particles, apply wall/boundary interactions and sample collisions within cells. A representative no-time-counter algorithm uses a bound on gσ_T for candidate selection and acceptance. Specify hard-sphere, VHS or another collision model, distinguishing Bird’s early construction from later algorithms.

Conditions and pitfalls

DSMC uses dilute-gas and molecular-chaos assumptions. Compare cell size with mean free path and step size with mean collision time; adequate resolution is problem dependent. In low-speed flow, the macroscopic signal can be buried in thermal noise, and longer averaging does not remove discretization bias.

What to check

Test homogeneous velocity relaxation, Maxwellian equilibrium, wall-driven Couette flow or a rarefied shock. Check collision-level momentum/energy conservation, cell/step/particle-count sensitivity and uncertainty accounting for correlated samples.

dae.title: Differential-algebraic equations / DAE
dae.html:
Differential-algebraic equations / DAE

A DAE combines differential evolution with algebraic constraints. An implicit ODE is not necessarily a DAE; singular dependence on derivatives is central to the distinction.

Problem and representative equations

Use F(t,y,ẏ)=0. A semi-explicit system ẋ=f(x,z,t), 0=g(x,z,t) with invertible g_z is a representative locally eliminable index-1 case. Several index definitions exist; differentiation index concerns differentiating constraints to obtain an explicit ODE.

F(t,y,y˙)=0,y˙n+1≈α0yn+1+∑j=1kαjyn+1−jΔt,JN=Fy+α0ΔtFy˙.F(t,y,\dot y)=0,\qquad \dot y_{n+1}\approx\frac{\alpha_0y_{n+1}+\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_jy_{n+1-j}}{\Delta t},\qquad J_N=F_y+\frac{\alpha_0}{\Delta t}F_{\dot y}.F(t,y,y˙​)=0,y˙​n+1​≈Δtα0​yn+1​+∑j=1k​αj​yn+1−j​​,JN​=Fy​+Δtα0​​Fy˙​​.

Algorithm

BDF methods approximate ẏ from the state history and solve F=0 using Newton iterations. The Newton matrix includes F_y+α₀F_ẏ/Δt. Initial values and derivatives must be consistent with both algebraic constraints and F(t₀,y₀,ẏ₀)=0.

Conditions and pitfalls

Higher-index systems can contain hidden constraints, drift and degraded error control, requiring index reduction or projection formulations. Smaller ODE time steps alone do not fix these issues. Scale tolerances separately for differential and algebraic variables and their units.

What to check

For an index-1 system with known solution, measure state error, F residual, algebraic-constraint violation and initialization consistency. Vary steps, nonlinear tolerances and initial perturbations; record constraint drift and termination reasons.

automatic-differentiation.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
automatic-differentiation.html:
Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers

Automatic differentiation (AD) evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the elementary operations in a program. It supplies Jacobians for Newton iterations, directional derivatives for Krylov methods, and sensitivities for parameter estimation. These are shared numerical foundations across many physical models.

Implemented here: a small forward-mode dual-number engine and a comparison of analytic differentiation, finite differences and AD on the existing Bratu boundary-value problem. The experiment reuses the atlas's Armijo-damped Newton solver. Reverse mode, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are explained as connections; this exhibit does not implement them.

Four ways to obtain a derivative

An analytic derivative is derived mathematically and entered into the solver by hand. It can expose structure and provide an independent reference, but the derivative must be kept consistent with the residual implementation. Symbolic differentiation manipulates expressions into another expression. AD instead carries numerical derivative information through the evaluated operations, without constructing a global symbolic formula.

Finite differences estimate a derivative from perturbed function values. For a vector residual F and a direction v, forward and centered differences are

Dε+F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u)ε,Dε0F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u−εv)2ε.D_\varepsilon^+F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u)}{\varepsilon}, \qquad D_\varepsilon^0F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u-\varepsilon v)}{2\varepsilon}.Dε+​F(u)v=εF(u+εv)−F(u)​,Dε0​F(u)v=2εF(u+εv)−F(u−εv)​.

For sufficiently smooth F, their truncation errors are first and second order in ε. A very small ε amplifies cancellation and rounding in the residual evaluations. The useful step depends on the state, direction, precision and scaling of F. A finite-difference check should therefore sweep several steps.

AD has no finite-difference step or associated truncation error. It still uses floating-point arithmetic: unstable formulas, overflow, underflow and rounding can affect both values and derivatives. The differentiated object is the composition of real-arithmetic operations represented by the executed program, evaluated numerically. It is not the derivative of the discontinuous mapping from one set of floating-point bit patterns to another.

Forward mode: carry a value and a direction

Seed the input with a direction v and propagate pairs consisting of a value and its directional derivative. Dual-number notation makes the chain rule visible:

a^=a+ηa˙,η2=0,a^b^=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp⁡(a^)=exp⁡(a)+ηexp⁡(a)a˙.\widehat a=a+\eta\dot a,\qquad \eta^2=0, \qquad \widehat a\widehat b=ab+\eta(\dot a b+a\dot b), \qquad \exp(\widehat a)=\exp(a)+\eta\exp(a)\dot a.a=a+ηa˙,η2=0,ab=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp(a)=exp(a)+ηexp(a)a˙.

The nilpotent symbol η is an algebraic device, not a small numerical step. The implementation stores the two arrays separately. It overloads the small set of operations needed for this experiment, including elementwise arithmetic, indexing, exponentiation and multiplication by a constant matrix. Unsupported operations are outside this educational engine's scope.

For F from n inputs to m outputs, one seeded execution returns F(u) and J(u)v. This Jacobian–vector product (JVP) avoids storing an m-by-n Jacobian. Seed each coordinate basis vector in turn to assemble all n columns. The Bratu comparison deliberately uses that transparent assembly; it does not exploit sparsity coloring or provide a matrix-free Newton solver.

Reverse mode and the derivative you actually need

Reverse mode propagates an output weight w backwards through local derivative rules to obtain J(u)ᵀw, often called a vector–Jacobian product (VJP). For a scalar objective with many parameters, one reverse pass can produce its gradient. An implementation commonly retains intermediate values or recomputes them through checkpointing. Forward mode is attractive when only a few input directions are required. The relevant dimensions are the numbers of independent inputs and outputs, together with the requested products.

A Hessian–vector product for a smooth scalar objective can be obtained by differentiating its gradient in a direction. Explicitly assembling a Hessian is unnecessary when an optimization method only needs that product. See Baydin et al. (2018) for an AD survey and the JAX autodiff cookbook for practical JVP, VJP and higher-order constructions. JAX is a reading reference; the local experiment requires only the atlas's existing NumPy environment.

The existing Bratu problem

We retain the same sign convention, parameter and exact solution used in the sparse and nonlinear systems verification:

−u′′(x)−λeu(x)=0,0<x<1,u(0)=u(1)=0,λ=2cosh⁡2(1/2),-u''(x)-\lambda e^{u(x)}=0,\qquad 0<x<1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0, \qquad \lambda=\frac{2}{\cosh^2(1/2)},−u′′(x)−λeu(x)=0,0<x<1,u(0)=u(1)=0,λ=cosh2(1/2)2​,
u∗(x)=−2log⁡ ⁣(cosh⁡(x−1/2)cosh⁡(1/2)).u_*(x)=-2\log\!\left(\frac{\cosh(x-1/2)}{\cosh(1/2)}\right).u∗​(x)=−2log(cosh(1/2)cosh(x−1/2)​).

Here n denotes the number of interior unknowns. The interval has n+1 uniform cells, with h=1/(n+1) and nodes x_i=ih. Centered differences give

Fi(u)=2ui−ui−1−ui+1h2−λeui,u0=un+1=0,F_i(u)=\frac{2u_i-u_{i-1}-u_{i+1}}{h^2}-\lambda e^{u_i}, \qquad u_0=u_{n+1}=0,Fi​(u)=h22ui​−ui−1​−ui+1​​−λeui​,u0​=un+1​=0,
J(u)=D−λdiag⁡(eu),D=1h2tridiag⁡(−1,2,−1).J(u)=D-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(e^u), \qquad D=\frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1).J(u)=D−λdiag(eu),D=h21​tridiag(−1,2,−1).

The analytic Jacobian is an independent formula. Finite differences and AD both evaluate the same residual function. In particular, AD differentiates the discrete residual F; it does not remove the centered stencil's spatial discretization error. The exact continuous solution is used to check spatial refinement, not as an exact root of the discrete equations.

Verification: hold the problem fixed

The saved measurements and source hashes separate three checks so that accurate derivatives and accurate PDE solutions are not confused.

The derivative check uses n=31 and the state u_*(x_i)+0.05 sin(3πx_i), away from the exact continuous profile. Its direction is sin(2πx_i)+0.3 cos(5πx_i), normalized to unit Euclidean length. The sweep contains 29 logarithmically spaced, absolute perturbations from 1 down to 10⁻¹⁴; these are derivative perturbations, not spatial mesh widths.

  1. Differentiate at a fixed state. Compare the assembled forward-mode AD Jacobian and its JVP against the analytic formula. Sweep finite-difference steps at that same state, using both forward and centered differences. Report relative Frobenius errors for matrices and relative Euclidean errors for directional products. A deterministic smooth direction prevents run-to-run changes in the comparison.
  2. Solve the same discrete system. Start every Newton solve at zero, use the same residual, Armijo search, dense linear solve and residual tolerance, and change only how the Jacobian is supplied. The finite-difference run uses a fixed centered-difference step recorded in the manifest. Measure the true residual after each accepted iteration and compare the final roots with the analytic-Jacobian solve.
  3. Refine the mesh. Repeat the three methods for n=15, 31 and 63 interior nodes. Compare their roots with u_* at the interior nodes using a nodal maximum error. Approximately fourfold error reduction under halving h identifies the centered scheme's second-order spatial behavior.

In the saved run, AD and the analytic Jacobian agree entry by entry, while the relative JVP error is about 8×10⁻¹⁶. This exact matrix agreement is specific to the operation ordering in this example, not a general guarantee of bitwise agreement for AD. The finite-difference curves show the useful range between truncation error and cancellation. All nine Newton solves reach the common absolute residual Euclidean tolerance 10⁻¹⁰ in three updates. The fixed centered-difference perturbation is 10⁻⁵; its final roots agree with the analytic-Jacobian roots to less than 10⁻¹⁴ in nodal maximum norm. The continuous nodal maximum errors are approximately 1.738×10⁻⁴, 4.337×10⁻⁵ and 1.084×10⁻⁵ on the three grids. Their factor-of-four reduction remains after changing the derivative calculation: spatial discretization sets the leading solution error here.

The matrix norm includes entries of size h⁻². A small relative matrix error can therefore hide errors in smaller terms. The direct directional check is reported separately, rather than relying only on a product of the assembled finite-difference matrix.

The analytic derivative is a reference, not an assumption that every analytic implementation is correct. The tests also check derivative rules on separate functions and nontrivial directions, and check Bratu refinement against the continuous solution. Agreement between two Jacobians alone would not validate the boundary conditions or the PDE discretization.

The figure makes no speed ranking. Assembling a dense AD Jacobian here needs n forward seeds; centered differences need two residual evaluations per column. Counts describe these implementations, not equal-cost operations or the best sparse AD strategy. For a large Newton–Krylov method, supplying Jv directly can be preferable to constructing every column, while a suitable preconditioner remains necessary.

Connections to implicit integration and parameter estimation

An implicit ODE stage has a residual involving the state and time step. Its Newton matrix contains derivatives of the ODE right-hand side, so the same AD construction can supply them. For parameter estimation, derivatives of observations or an objective with respect to model parameters connect a simulation to an optimization method. Derivative availability does not itself choose a stable integrator, a well-conditioned parameterization or a convergent optimization algorithm.

Suppose the converged discrete state satisfies F(u,θ)=0. At a differentiable solution with nonsingular F_u, its parameter sensitivity satisfies

Fududθ=−Fθ.F_u\frac{du}{d\theta}=-F_\theta.Fu​dθdu​=−Fθ​.

For a scalar objective L(u,θ), an adjoint solve gives

FuTp=LuT,dLdθ=Lθ−pTFθ.F_u^T p=L_u^T,\qquad \frac{dL}{d\theta}=L_\theta-p^TF_\theta.FuT​p=LuT​,dθdL​=Lθ​−pTFθ​.

This differentiates the equation defining the solution. Differentiating a fixed, finite sequence of Newton iterations instead gives the derivative of that sequence, including its dependence on the initial guess. Stopping criteria and line-search branches complicate that distinction. Near a singular Jacobian, sensitivities can be large even when the primal residual is small. Primal and derivative solve tolerances therefore need separate checks. These sensitivity and adjoint equations are explanatory extensions; the present Bratu exhibit compares Jacobians used in the primal solve.

Limits: smoothness, branches and numerical stability

AD applies the derivative rules of the operations that are executed. At a branch boundary, an absolute-value corner or a limiter switch, the underlying function may have no unique classical derivative; a library's chosen rule does not establish one. Adaptive time-step decisions can change the executed path under parameter perturbations. For shocks, a computed grid-value derivative also needs interpretation in terms of shock motion and the quantity being measured.

The discretized derivative should be checked for mesh and time-step convergence when it is intended to approximate a continuous sensitivity. Differentiating a discretized solver and discretizing continuous sensitivity or adjoint equations require their own consistency analysis. Stable function evaluation matters too: a formula that overflows in the primal calculation is not repaired by applying the chain rule.

Reproduce the comparison

Extract the November 22, 2026 release ZIP into a new folder. Prepare a Python environment with NumPy, Matplotlib and pytest, and run from the extracted folder. See the README for the complete instructions.

python -m pip install numpy matplotlib pytest
python scripts/build_autodiff.py
python -m pytest tests/test_autodiff.py

Read the AD engine and Bratu residual, existing Newton solver, figure and evidence builder, and test source individually. An independent-extraction verification record and source inventory and hashes accompany the package.

The builder writes the figure and a JSON manifest containing grids, parameters, finite-difference steps, stopping controls, norms, solver histories, the numerical environment and source SHA-256 hashes. Evidence is generated from the numerical implementation independently of the website build. The dated supplement includes the forward-mode engine, Bratu comparison, tests and saved results introduced here. Reverse-mode and adjoint solvers remain outside this implementation. Continue with Newton and conditioning, stiff integration, or the error-norm guide.

Implicit differentiation and adjoints: verified Bratu sensitivity

Executable implicit state sensitivities and discrete adjoints are now provided in the separate Bratu parameter-sensitivity chapter. This does not expand the earlier forward-mode release; a separate dated supplement checks root sensitivity and total objective derivatives.

Publication scope and related entries

A separate November 22, 2026 supplement fixes its source, tests, figure and JSON evidence. Reverse mode, Hessian-vector products, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are reading connections rather than implemented solvers in this exhibit. pinn-operators.title: PINNs and neural operators
pinn-operators.html:
PINNs and neural operators

A PINN fits a neural representation of a particular solution; a neural operator learns a map from input functions such as coefficients or initial data to solution functions. Their targets and validation protocols differ.

Problem and representative equations

A PINN minimizes an empirical weighted loss of PDE, boundary and data residuals. N and B are differential/boundary operators and f,g are prescribed data. A representative FNO layer combines a Fourier-parameterized integral operator K with a local map W acting on feature functions v.

L(θ)=λr⟨∣N[uθ]−f∣2⟩r+λb⟨∣B[uθ]−g∣2⟩b+λd⟨∣uθ−uobs∣2⟩d.\mathcal L(\theta)=\lambda_r\langle|\mathcal N[u_\theta]-f|^2\rangle_r+\lambda_b\langle|\mathcal B[u_\theta]-g|^2\rangle_b+\lambda_d\langle|u_\theta-u_{\rm obs}|^2\rangle_d.L(θ)=λr​⟨∣N[uθ​]−f∣2⟩r​+λb​⟨∣B[uθ​]−g∣2⟩b​+λd​⟨∣uθ​−uobs​∣2⟩d​.
vℓ+1=σ ⁣(Wℓvℓ+F−1[Kℓ Fvℓ]).v_{\ell+1}=\sigma\!\left(W_\ell v_\ell+\mathcal F^{-1}[K_\ell\,\mathcal Fv_\ell]\right).vℓ+1​=σ(Wℓ​vℓ​+F−1[Kℓ​Fvℓ​]).

Algorithm

For a PINN, scale coordinates/units, differentiate residuals, specify collocation points and boundary enforcement, and optimize. FNO trains an operator on input/reference-solution pairs and truncates Fourier modes. Cite the PINN and FNO papers as separate proposals.

Conditions and pitfalls

Small training loss is not a bound on global solution error or conservation. Examine residual imbalance, shocks, stiff scales and out-of-distribution inputs. Transfer between discretizations is not a guarantee of physical correctness at arbitrary resolution.

What to check

Compare against analytic or independently converged conventional solutions. Measure off-training L1/L2/L∞ errors, boundaries, conservation and multiple seeds. Split operator data by independent problems rather than nearby time slices alone, and report distribution-shift tests separately.

Publication scope and related entries

rotated-hybrid.title: Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver
rotated-hybrid.html:
Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver

Rotated Riemann methods construct dissipation using directions beyond the face normal. Ren’s rotated Roe method (2003) and Nishikawa–Kitamura’s rotated-hybrid method (2008) are related but distinct.

Problem and representative equations

For 2D Euler states U_L,U_R and unit face normal n, resolve n into orthogonal unit directions n₁,n₂ with weights αᵢ=n·nᵢ. The formula below defines this atlas’s educational HLLE/Roe experiment, not the optimized dissipation formula in the 2008 paper.

n=α1n1+α2n2,F^(n)=α1F^HLLE(n1)+α2F^Roe(n2).\mathbf n=\alpha_1\mathbf n_1+\alpha_2\mathbf n_2,\qquad\widehat F(\mathbf n)=\alpha_1\widehat F_{\rm HLLE}(\mathbf n_1)+\alpha_2\widehat F_{\rm Roe}(\mathbf n_2).n=α1​n1​+α2​n2​,F(n)=α1​FHLLE​(n1​)+α2​FRoe​(n2​).

Algorithm

The implementation aligns n₁ with the velocity jump, orienting directions to have nonnegative projections on the face normal. A tiny jump falls back to the face tangent. Rotate the same states into each frame, evaluate HLLE/Roe, rotate momentum fluxes back and combine. This differs from a pressure-sensor flux blend.

Conditions and pitfalls

Roe (1981) supplies the component approximate solver. The 2003 rotated-method paper is by Y.-X. Ren; the 2008 rotated-hybrid paper is by Hiroaki Nishikawa and Keiichi Kitamura. Roe, Nishikawa, Ismail and Scalabrin (2005) is related carbuncle research, not the authorship/date of that 2008 paper. No universal carbuncle or positivity guarantee is claimed here.

What to check

Check constant states, flux reversal under state/normal exchange and rotational covariance. Separate normal compression from pure tangential shear, then compare perturbed planar shocks and blunt-body cases under fixed conditions. Link the dated package’s actual tests/results without claiming a new reproduction of the papers.

Publication scope and related entries

low-mach-preconditioning.html:
Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes

Separate acoustic/convective preconditioning from transonic numerical-viscosity corrections. Connect a concrete Γ, a linear eigenvalue model, Mach cutoffs and dual time stepping with explicit variable conventions.

Matrix-solve and PDE preconditioning

Left preconditioning P⁻¹Ax=P⁻¹b assists an iterative linear solve. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning instead changes pseudo-time mass matrices or characteristic numerical dissipation. Papers may use P for both; identify the operator being modified first.

At low Mach number, |u_n±a| is large compared with convection |u_n|, affecting steady iteration and low-speed flux accuracy. This is a different limit from a transonic characteristic u_n±a=0.

Place Γ on pseudo time

Distinguish conservative U from primitive q and pseudo time τ from physical time t. Steady problems omit the physical-time term. Unsteady dual-time iterations retain the physically discretized term, such as BDF2, throughout the inner solve. Γ is not the same matrix as U_q.

For nonsingular Γ and unchanged R, a converged steady pseudo-time solve still satisfies R=0. Preconditioning spatial dissipation additionally changes the discrete residual construction. Indiscriminately preconditioning physical time changes the unsteady solution, including acoustics.

Setting U_ref=a gives Θ=ρ/p and recovers the physical Jacobian U_q in this ordering. Reducing U_ref toward a convective scale changes pseudo-acoustic scales. Γ, its inverse and a conservative-variable P are not numerically identical matrices.

Stagnation singularities and a Mach cutoff

A representative bounded parameter is shown below. Positive M_cut prevents U_ref=0 at stagnation; the upper bound recovers the physical system at supersonic speed. This is an illustrative choice, not a universal prescription: viscous, unsteady and boundary-aware variants use other reference scales.

The cutoff avoids degeneracy of the preconditioner near zero velocity; it does not remove physical Mach-1 flow from the domain. Too large a cutoff weakens low-Mach benefits; too small a value can impair robustness or boundary behavior.

To expose the effect, linearize about constant density/sound speed and use pressure perturbation divided by ρ₀a, normal/tangential velocities and an advected entropy variable with fixed scaling. The following P is an illustrative pressure-row scaling, not the nonlinear Γ above.

The model has zero acoustic eigenvalue product when u_n²=a². More generally, multiplication by an invertible P cannot remove singularity of A. Sonic singularities of particular attempts at isotropic acoustic preconditioning also require formulation-specific discussion.

Transonic rarefaction and an entropy fix

A Roe linearization can produce an unphysical expansion shock when a characteristic crosses zero through a rarefaction. A representative smoothing replaces |λ| in the numerical dissipation as below. δ has speed units; state-aware choices and fixed fractional cutoffs are different variants.

This modifies numerical viscosity rather than deleting the physical characteristic. The published acoustic quadratic smoothing is not claimed as a faithful reproduction of every Harten–Hyman construction. Entropy correction, HLLE low-density robustness, carbuncle control and low-Mach preconditioning address different problems.

Checks that keep the mechanisms separate

Test spectra, recovery at β→1, low-Mach scaling and near-stagnation invertibility on small linear problems. Measure pseudo-time convergence separately from solution error due to changed spatial fluxes. Interior eigenvalue analysis alone cannot assess boundary reflection.

Use transonic Burgers/Euler rarefactions to examine expansion shocks, refinement and δ sensitivity. For unsteady problems separate physical-time convergence from inner pseudo-residual convergence. Low-Mach checks here are proposed work; existing Jacobi scaling or dual-time examples do not validate a dedicated low-Mach flow solver.

steady-runge-kutta.title: Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions
steady-runge-kutta.html:
Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions

Interpret multistage pseudo-time iterations as smoothers for a steady residual. A Jameson–Schmidt–Turkel-family example connects stage coefficients, stability polynomials, nonlinear order, high-frequency damping and preconditioning.

The target is R(U)=0, not a physical-time trajectory

For a discrete steady Euler/Navier–Stokes residual R, iterate an artificial ODE in pseudo time τ toward its root. Here R is the conservative residual divided by cell volume. The step is a pseudo-time step; the aim is an adequately converged residual and steady observables, not an accurate physical transient.

The following base-state recurrence forms every stage from the same U^(0), unlike chaining forward-Euler increments from the preceding stage. Compare coefficients only after matching residual sign, cell-volume scaling and any preconditioning action.

dUdτ=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αkΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s).\frac{dU}{d\tau}=-R(U),\quad U^{(0)}=U^n,\quad U^{(k)}=U^{(0)}-\alpha_k\Delta\tau R(U^{(k-1)}),\quad U^{n+1}=U^{(s)}.dτdU​=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αk​ΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s).

A representative Jameson-family four-stage iteration

Consider these coefficients with the same autonomous residual reevaluated at every stage. For R(U)=AU, the stability polynomial equals classical RK4. The simplified recurrence is not a complete specification of the original fluxes, artificial dissipation and dissipation-update schedule.

Equality of linear stability polynomials does not establish nonlinear fourth-order physical-time accuracy. This base-state recurrence is generally second order for nonlinear autonomous ODEs: it fails the third-order condition bᵀ(c⊙c)=1/3. Distinguish its steady-solver purpose and nonlinear order conditions from classical RK4.

Stability and high-frequency damping are different

For linearized residual modes, the iteration multiplier is a stability polynomial. |ℛ|≤1 prevents growth, but |ℛ| near one barely damps error. A multigrid smoother seeks small maximum amplification μ on frequencies H not representable on the coarse grid.

For a purely decaying z=−2 mode, this four-stage polynomial gives ℛ=1/3, while near-zero low-frequency modes decay slowly. Pushing the step to a stability boundary does not maximize damping or minimize time to convergence. Advection and diffusion occupy different spectral regions.

Residual smoothing, preconditioning and multigrid

Residual smoothing is a separate spatial filtering operation, not the choice of RK stage coefficients. With dimensionless centered D₂ on a uniform periodic grid and ε≥0, the example below attenuates high-frequency residuals. An invertible filter retains the residual root but changes the iteration spectrum.

Low-Mach preconditioning changes acoustic/convective scales, local stepping changes per-cell iteration increments, and coarse correction treats errors poorly reduced by the smoother. Combined iterations still require boundary/variable-coefficient/nonnormality analysis and must be distinguished from physical-time integration.

Measure residuals, steady observables and work

Measure Fourier-mode damping on a manufactured Poisson-type problem and compare with μ. For compressible flow track true residuals scaled by conservative component and steady quantities such as forces, mass flow and conservation balances. When smoothing residuals, also display the original unsmoothed residual.

Report residual evaluations and linear-solve work, final errors and termination reasons, not only stage/cycle counts. Compare methods at the same steady solution and tolerance. This chapter supplies algorithmic reading, not a dedicated Jameson solver or new flow-validation results.

h2-hf.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
h2-hf.html:
Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement

Solve two-electron H₂ at fixed proton positions using original s-Gaussian integrals and restricted closed-shell Hartree–Fock (RHF). Energy stabilization, satisfaction of the discrete SCF equations, changes under basis expansion and physical accuracy are separate questions.

This implementation covers isolated two-electron H2 RHF in finite s-only bases. It does not implement general molecular HF, establish a complete-basis limit, recover the correlated dissociation curve, or supply molecular/periodic DFT.

Fixed input, code, tests and acceptance · ZIP · Independent-extraction verification / JSON

The model being solved

This is a Born–Oppenheimer electronic problem with the internuclear distance R fixed by the input. Atomic units are used: distances in bohr and energies in hartree. Relativistic effects, nuclear motion, vibration/rotation, solvent and periodic boundaries are excluded. Total energy including nuclear repulsion 1/R is recorded separately from electronic energy.

The two electrons occupy the same spatial orbital with opposite spins in closed-shell RHF. The same restriction is retained at stretched geometries. SCF convergence and agreement with another implementation do not establish the correct dissociation limit or recover electron correlation. This is not a switch to UHF, configuration interaction or DFT.

Sources: Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951), C. A. Coulson and I. Fischer (1949)

Gaussian basis functions and original integrals

Normalized s-type Gaussians centered on the two nuclei form the basis. A contracted function combines several exponents and coefficients, with normalization also applied to the contraction. Three primitives in STO-3G describe one contracted s function, not three independent basis functions. Inputs and results retain exponents, coefficients and contractions. The STO-3G numerical convention is checked against Basis Set Exchange version 1, rather than presented as a direct transcription of the original paper’s printed digits.

The educational code computes overlap S, kinetic T, nuclear attraction V and electron-repulsion integrals, defining the one-electron matrix as h=T+V. The s-type Coulomb integrals involve the Boys function F₀, which tends to 1 as t approaches zero. Direct evaluation of erf(√t)/√t at zero would produce 0/0, so the limiting region needs a stable treatment. The chemists’ integral index convention and spin-summed density P determine the factor 1/2 in exchange.
